title: Is rational solvability of polynomial equations decidable?
formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, given any integer-coefficient polynomial f(X₁,…,Xₘ), always halts and correctly decides whether $\exists (q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m:f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0$? The number of variables and polynomial degree are unrestricted parts of the finite input.
definitions: Encode m≥1 and a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an m-tuple of nonnegative binary exponents. Repeated monomials may be combined effectively; zero polynomials are allowed. A rational solution consists of exact fractions qᵢ=aᵢ/bᵢ, where aᵢ∈ℤ and bᵢ is a positive integer, with no prescribed bound on numerators or denominators. The required algorithm is one finite deterministic program, independent of m, degree, and coefficients. It must return yes exactly when a rational zero exists and no otherwise; it may use any finite amount of time and space on each input. Malformed encodings are rejected. The task supplies no oracle, height inequalities, integrality constraints on the unknowns, or promise of a solution. Rational coefficients would give an equivalent problem by clearing coefficient denominators. A finite system f₁=⋯=fᵣ=0 is equivalent over ℚ to the single equation f₁²+⋯+fᵣ²=0.
answer_criterion: Answer yes with a total correct decision algorithm for every such polynomial. Answer no by proving that no such Turing machine exists, for example through a computable reduction from the halting problem. A procedure that finds a solution whenever one exists but can run forever on no-instances is only a semidecision procedure and does not answer yes.
context:
Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of ℤ inside ℚ would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. Koenigsmann instead gives a universal definition of the integers, which is a major advance in definability but uses a different quantifier form. The full first-order theory of ℚ is already undecidable; the unresolved target concerns its existential fragment. An existential definition of ℤ is a sufficient route to a negative answer, not a condition that every possible negative solution must satisfy.

Recent results settle the analogous problem over the ring of integers of every number field. A ring of integers restricts denominators; it is not the whole number field. In particular the ring of integers of ℚ is ℤ, so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. Poonen’s July 2026 account explains how rank stability of abelian varieties yields the required Diophantine definitions for those rings.

Other nearby formulations add conditions comparing heights of rational coordinates. Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove an undecidability result with finitely many such conditions. Their formulation includes predicates absent here, and their paper explicitly retains ordinary Hilbert’s tenth problem over ℚ as open. This distinction matters when interpreting a result whose title refers to undecidable effectivity for rational points.
why: This is a fundamental boundary between algorithmic arithmetic and undecidability. It asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver, connecting computation, logical definability, and the arithmetic geometry of rational points.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively. The rational-solution analogue remains distinct.
Koenigsmann gives a universal first-order definition of ℤ in ℚ and related low-quantifier undecidability results. This does not supply an existential definition.
Anscombe and coauthors survey local-global methods and explicitly identify Hilbert’s tenth problem over number fields, including ℚ, as open.
Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove undecidability after adjoining finitely many height-comparison conditions. Those extra conditions are not part of ordinary rational solvability.

Rank-stability advances imply undecidability over rings of integers of all number fields. Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the proof and gives an alternative Diophantine-definability argument; the domains remain rings of integers.

status_note: Explicitly open in the cited rational-solvability and local-global sources. Research through 10 September 2026 found no resolution over ℚ. The recent results for rings of integers and for additional height predicates do not answer this formulation.
